newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarians outraged at exhibition on Hitler's army.
newsitem.headline: Bavarians outraged at exhibition on Hitler's army.

text.p: Bavaria's ruling conservatives are up in arms about a forthcoming exhibition in Munich challenging the notion that the regular German army had nothing to do with the worst excesses of the Nazis.

The official newspaper of the Christian Social Union (CSU), which rules the southern German state with an absolute majority, this week accused the exhibition due to open in Munich city hall on Monday of "defaming the German people".
"It's unbelievable how parts of the CSU, right up to the party newspaper, are drifting to the right wing," Munich's Social Democrat mayor Christian Ude said on Thursday.
"There are no clear boundaries to be seen between them and right-wing radical groups."

The CSU finds itself in the company of neo-Nazis in opposing "War of Extermination -- Crimes of the Wehrmacht 1941-1944", an exhibition by the Hamburg Institute for Social Research documenting the atrocities of Hitler's Wehrmacht.

Munich CSU leader Peter Gauweiler has even suggested Jan Philipp Reemtsma, the institute's patron who used to own one of Germany's biggest tobacco firms, would be better advised to stage an exhibtion on people who have died from smoking.
"This is a very cynical attempt to put the victims of National Socialist (Nazi) atrocities in the same category as the victims of the health risks of a stimulant," Ude said.

The exhibition uses photographs and letters from soldiers themselves to back up its premise that the regular army also participated in mass killings of the Jews and other atrocities, not just the SS units usually blamed for war crimes.
The exhibition stirred up a big debate when it was unveiled in Hamburg two years ago but has since toured more than a dozen German cities provoking little controversy.
But Munich, which had the status of "Capital city of the Movement" during the Nazi era, is proving very different.
Right-wing extremists plan a demonstration on March 1 against the exhibition under the title "Our grandfathers were no criminals -- and we're proud of them!".
Ude branded the demonstration "particularly tasteless" because of the route the organisers have chosen.

It is due to begin in a square named in honour of Hans and Sophie Scholl, a brother and sister executed for leading an anti-Nazi group during the Third Reich, and end at the Feldherrenhalle, a favourite rallying point of the Nazis.

Ude said he was looking at ways to restrict the protest but added: "The right of freedom to demonstrate applies also to those whose views are irrelevant, tasteless and politically intolerable, as long as they don't commit any crimes."
Supporters of the exhibition, including the Social Democrats, Greens, trade unionists and church groups, plan a counter-demonstration.
